tweets.text:
The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. 

Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before.

What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before.

If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems.

Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

"Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully"

Due to how we use RL for LLMs, there is currently little incentive for models to admit uncertainty, preventing them to guess even when they're unlikely to succeed.

This paper GracefulRL instead trains models to prefer success over safe fallback, and safe fallback over failure. They did it by using a modified RL objective that prevents the model from collapsing into always refusing.

On AIME, it reduces incorrect answers from 79.1% to 8.9%, while sacrificing only 3.1% of correct answers. On Minesweeper, it even improves success from 67.4% to 77.4% while reducing errors.

https://t.co/0POjtcbgXz

"Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting"

Long-running AI research agents plateau as their context accumulates. It also becomes more conservative and make smaller changes instead of exploring new ideas.

So this paper proposes forgetting, where you have the model periodically discarding all agent sessions and experiment histories, keeping only the best solution found so far. A fresh team of agents then resumes exploring from that solution.

Across four coding and optimization tasks, this improves performance by 10% on average over parallel agents, and 22% over a single agent at the same budget.

https://t.co/pSqNkziJDU
